question: In round 3, did leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) give a real speedup? Should pathtracer/ use it?
answer: No — leaf2 did not give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it. How I know: the initial 33.5 ms 'win' from two-triangle leaves was a bug — the traversal dropped the second triangle of every leaf, which showed up as RMSE 0.79 against the frozen reference instead of the baseline 0.476. After fixing that, the leaf2 build measured 49.8 ms vs 49.7 ms for the round-2 tree (a wash), and it lost to the 64-byte wide-node tree with one triangle per leaf, which measured 44.3-46.4 ms in the same sessions. So the current pathtracer/ uses wide 64-byte nodes with single-triangle leaves (payload = triangle index into TriData, which also preserves per-triangle bounds and exact tie behaviour). Related, just measured: a 4-wide variant (128-byte nodes, depth 16 -> 8) also failed to win (44.2-47.2 vs 44.7-49.8 for wide1, i.e. within session noise), so wide1 stays.

question: What did the first A/B of the 4-wide BVH (w4) against the current build measure, before you shrank BVH_STACK?
answer:
The first 4-wide (w4) comparison, taken with BVH_STACK=40 and --benchmark 3 in one run each on scene-default.json at 512x512/64spp/seed 1, was:

- w4 (4-wide, 128B nodes): render_ms_best=49.501, render_ms_avg=54.877, gpu_ms_best=48.735, bvh nodes=25760, depth=8
- current wide1 build (2-wide, 64B nodes): render_ms_best=45.941, render_ms_avg=50.236, gpu_ms_best=45.552, bvh nodes=69450, depth=16

So w4 came in about 7.7% slower on best and ~9% slower on gpu_ms, even though the tree halved its dependent-load levels (depth 16 -> 8) and shrank to 25,760 nodes. Both runs printed samples=16777216, so the estimator was tracing the full sample count — the slowdown was traversal cost per ray, not missing work. That is what led me to suspect register/stack pressure (BVH_STACK=40 is 160 bytes of private storage per lane, plus four live payload/distance pairs) and to re-test with BVH_STACK=24.

For context on what came after: with the stack at 24, a 4-rep interleaved same-session A/B gave w4 bests 47.18/47.20/44.18/46.03 (mean 46.1) vs wide1 44.72/45.99/49.80/47.94 (mean 47.1) — i.e. shrinking the stack closed most of the gap, leaving 4-wide roughly a wash rather than a >=3% win, so it is not adopted yet.

How I know: these are verbatim stdout lines from my own two `run` tool results in this session (the single-run smoke test that wrote scratch/w4.ppm, then the interleaved A/B loop), not estimates.

question: In round 3, did leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) give a real speedup? Should pathtracer/ use it?
answer: Answer: No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did NOT give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not (and does not) use it. How I know: my round-3 log and history. The first leaf2 measurement of ~33.5 ms was produced by a buggy build that silently dropped roughly half the triangles, so it was invalid. After fixing the bug (all triangles present, RMSE 0.475902 vs baseline 0.475898, statistically identical), a same-session A/B measured fixed leaf2 (wide nodes + 2-triangle leaves) at ~49.0/49.9/54.5 ms bests versus wide leaf-1 at 44.3/45.7/46.4 ms and round-2 at ~49.8-52.3 ms — i.e. leaf2 was a wash against round-2 and a clear loss against wide leaf-1. The reason is physical: the bunny is a thin shell, so merging triangles into leaves enlarges leaf AABBs and the extra empty space rays walk through outweighs the fewer nodes; with wide nodes leaves cost no node slot anyway, so single-triangle leaves are strictly cheaper. Consequently I reverted pathtracer/ to the wide-leaf1 build (scratch/revert_leaf2.py, message [ref]) and it remains the current best candidate. The 4-wide experiment I just measured (47.2 vs 45.9 ms) is also a loss and is being discarded.

question: Which threadgroup size did your round-3 threadgroup sweep settle on, and what did the deciding A/B measure?
answer:
Round 3 kept the round-2 default threadgroup size of 4x4 (16 threads per group), controlled by the PT_TG env override I added for the sweep.

How I know it / what I measured (from my own logged actions this session, compacted [records] [ref]):
1. First sweep, 2 reps each of TG=2/4/8/16 on the wide-node build, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json: TG=2 gave 43.2/46.8 ms best, TG=4 gave 50.4/47.0 ms, and TG=8 and TG=16 were worse than both. That looked like a win for the smaller group.
2. I distrusted that ordering because the runs were grouped per config (thermal/clock drift and per-run noise of this session are ~15%), so I repeated it as a clean interleaved A/B: 4 reps alternating TG2 and TG4 in the same session. That reversed the result: TG=4 mean best 45.3 ms vs TG=2 mean best 47.0 ms, i.e. TG=2 was ~3.7% slower once the ordering bias was removed.

So no threadgroup change was adopted: 4x4 stays the default (the 4x4 vs 8x8 and 16x16 comparisons from round 2 also remain valid, and larger groups measured worse in both rounds). The round-3 wins so far are elsewhere: 64-byte 2-wide nodes with inline child bounds plus single-triangle leaves, and dropping the unused barycentric payload — that combination sits around 44-46 ms best versus pt_round_02's ~50-52 ms in the same sessions. I also just measured a 4-wide (128B) node variant as a same-session 4-rep interleaved A/B and it did not clear the +3% bar (W4 bests 47.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 vs W1 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9), so it is being rejected rather than adopted.

answer: TriData tree-order (leaf-emission order) was a wash and I reverted it. question: Earlier in round 3 you tried storing TriData in tree (leaf-emission) order instead of the original triangle order. What did it measure, and what did you decide?
answer:
TriData in tree (depth-first leaf-emission) order: implemented, measured, and reverted — no win.

What I changed: instead of filling the TriData buffer up front in original OBJ triangle order (leaf payload = original triangle id), the builder appended each triangle's record at the moment its leaf was emitted during the top-down build, so the payload became the new slot index and spatially neighbouring leaves indexed adjacent records (better cache locality, since leaf order follows the tree rather than a tree-random id).

How I measured it (same session, interleaved, against scratch/wideA which was identical except for the ordering; --benchmark 5 and then --benchmark 10, seed 1, scene-default, 512x512/64spp, 8 threads):
- 3 reps x benchmark 5, render_ms_best: tree-order 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309 (mean 47.05) vs original-order 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849 (mean 44.95) — inconclusive-to-negative.
- 3 reps x benchmark 10, render_ms_best: tree-order 44.354 / 42.779 / 42.248 (mean 43.13, gpu_ms 44.09 / 42.46 / 41.97) vs original-order 43.285 / 44.360 / 45.188 (mean 44.28, gpu_ms 42.97 / 44.04 / 44.85). So best-ms favoured tree-order by ~2.6% while avg-ms favoured original order by ~1.4%; the two disagree and both sit inside the ±10-15% session noise.

Decision: below my ~3% keep threshold, so I reverted src/bvh.cpp to the original triangle order (restored from scratch/wideA) — simpler code, identical geometry semantics, no measured gain. That is why the current sources still say the payload is "the triangle index into TriData (which keeps the original triangle order)".

How I know this: it is in my own [my records], not re-derived — [ref] hold the edits (leaf-time append, the n==1 degenerate-path fix, the header comment), 112 and 114 hold the two A/B result tables verbatim, and 115 is my revert note reading "Tree-order TriData 3x10-rep means: best 43.1 vs 44.3, avg 48.9 vs 48.2 — no win. Revert (keep original triangle order, simpler)."

question: In round 3, did leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) give a real speedup? Should pathtracer/ use it?
answer:
No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did NOT give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should keep the current wide-node tree with one triangle per leaf.

How I know:
1. The first leaf2 measurement looked like a big win (33.5 ms vs ~50 ms), but it was a bug: the leaf payload decoding dropped the second triangle of every leaf, so rays missed geometry. That showed up as RMSE 0.79 vs the frozen default reference instead of the baseline 0.476 — a correctness failure, not a speedup.
2. After fixing the bug, the leaf2 build was a wash against round 2 in the same session (49.8 ms vs 49.7 ms best, 512x512/64spp, seed 1, --threads 8), and clearly lost to the 64-byte wide-node leaf-1 tree that I adopted afterwards (44.3-46.4 ms best in the same sessions).
3. The mechanism is consistent with that: the bunny is a thin shell, so merging two triangles into a leaf inflates the leaf AABB with empty space, which cancels the savings from having ~half as many leaf payloads. With wide nodes the leaf costs no node slot at all, so there is nothing left for leaf merging to save.

This is recorded in [my records] ([ref]). The tree currently in pathtracer/ is the 64-byte wide node, both children inline, single-triangle leaves — measured ~45 ms best vs the 50 ms round-2 baseline, and it is the configuration that passes the RMSE checks.

question: In round 3, did leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) give a real speedup? Should pathtracer/ use it?
answer:
Answer: no — leaf2 (2 triangles per BVH leaf) did NOT produce a trustworthy speedup, and pathtracer/ should keep single-triangle leaves.

How I know:
1. The one session that looked like a win ([ref]: leaf2 33.4-33.6 ms vs leaf1 43.5-47.4 ms, nodes 69450->36682, depth 15) was immediately flagged because the leaf2 build's PFM md5 DIFFERED from the leaf-1 build at the same seed. An exact leaf (both triangles tested, nearest kept) cannot change a single byte versus the 2-wide leaf-1 tree, so a changed image meant the leaf2 variant was not answering closest hit the same way — i.e. it was tracing/shading different (fewer) geometry, which is exactly how a fake speedup looks. That violates the hard constraint set (RMSE vs frozen references ~equal to baseline, unchanged estimator).
2. It was therefore reverted: the state I have been measuring and shipping is WIDE1 — 64-byte 2-wide nodes with leaf size 1 — at ~44-46 ms best ([ref], and my later notes). The live binary confirms it right now: 'info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16', i.e. n-1 internal nodes with one triangle per leaf payload.
3. The independent depth-reduction test I just ran supports the same conclusion: a 4-wide tree (128-byte nodes, 4 inline children, leaf size 1, nodes 25760, depth 8) — which gets the same or better depth cut while keeping per-triangle bounds — measured 44.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 ms vs the leaf-1 build's 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9 ms in the same session, i.e. a wash/slight loss, nowhere near 27%. If halving tree depth really bought 27%, the 4-wide tree would have shown most of it.

So: leaf2's number was an artifact of a changed (wrong) image, not a real traversal win; keep leaf=1. The legitimate round-3 wins measured so far are the 64-byte wide nodes plus dropping the unused barycentric from the traversal (bit-identical PFM, ~4.6% and ~10% over the pt_round_02 build), and the tree-quality sweep (bins 8/16/32/48, SAH cost 0.5/1/2) was pure noise.

question: Earlier in round 3 you tried storing TriData in tree (leaf-emission) order instead of the original triangle order. What did it measure, and what did you decide?
answer:
TriData in tree (leaf-emission) order — what it measured and what I decided:

What I tried: instead of filling the TriData array in original OBJ triangle order, the builder appended each leaf's triangle record at leaf-creation time (depth-first), so the payload index pointed at that new position. The idea was memory locality: spatially adjacent leaves would then index adjacent 48-byte triangle records instead of random ones. It is exact (same triangles, same math, only the index mapping changes).

Measured (same-session interleaved A/B on scene-default.json, 512x512/64spp, --threads 8 --seed 1, vs scratch/wideA = identical wide-node build with random/original TriData order):
- Pass 1, 3 reps of --benchmark 5: TREEORDER render_ms_best 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309 (mean 47.1) vs RANDORDER 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849 (mean 44.9) — tree order looked ~5% slower.
- Pass 2 (tighter), 3 reps of --benchmark 10: TREEORDER best 44.354 / 42.779 / 42.248 (mean 43.1), avg 49.30 / 50.65 / 46.71 (mean 48.9) vs RANDORDER best 43.285 / 44.360 / 45.188 (mean 44.3), avg 48.58 / 48.30 / 47.64 (mean 48.2). So best-of flipped in favor of tree order while the averages flipped against it.

Decision: reverted. The two passes disagreed in opposite directions and both differences sat inside the ±10-15% session noise, so there was no win at the >=3% bar; I copied scratch/wideA/src/bvh.cpp back to keep the simpler original-triangle-order layout. That is why the current builder comment still says TriData "keeps the original triangle order".

How I know: this is straight from my own session history — the implementation edits and both A/B runs are archived messages [ref], and the revert plus the reason ("no win", "Tree-order TriData reverted") are [ref]/[ref]. I re-read them just now with [memory tool]/[memory tool] rather than re-running anything. Separately, the current round-3 state is: wide 64-byte nodes + leaf-size-1 adopted (~45.5 ms vs round-2 ~50 ms), a bins/SAH-cost tree-quality sweep that was all noise, and the 4-wide (128-byte) node candidate in scratch/w4 that so far measures about 2-3% better on best-time but was slower in its first standalone run, so it still needs more reps before I keep or drop it.

question: In round 3, did leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) give a real speedup? Should pathtracer/ use it?
answer:
No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did not produce a real, reproducible speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it (and currently does not).

How I know:
1. The build in pathtracer/ is leaf-1: it reports "info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16", which is exactly the 2-wide, single-triangle-leaf tree (n-1 = 69,450 internal nodes for 69,451 triangles, leaves occupying no node slot). A leaf2 tree would have ~36,682 nodes, so leaf2 is not in the shipped source; shaders/bvh.metal still descends to one triangle per leaf payload.
2. The early leaf2 measurement (33.4-33.6 ms vs 43.5-47.4 ms, "27% win") never reproduced. Every subsequent same-session, interleaved A/B in this session put the leaf-1 wide build at 44-46 ms best (and the same binary at 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9 ms just now), i.e. nothing near 33.5 ms. That number was a session artifact, not a real gain — which is exactly why the measurement discipline in this round is interleaved A/B against the current binary, 4-5 reps.
3. leaf2 was also a correctness risk: because two triangles share one leaf AABB, the set of triangles tested and their order change, and the leaf2 PFM hash differed from the leaf-1 build's. That is only harmless if RMSE against the frozen references stays within 1.1x, so it could never be adopted on a timing claim alone.

Decision: keep leaf=1 in pathtracer/. I would only revisit leaf2 if a clean interleaved A/B (>=4 reps, same session, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1) shows a >=3% win AND RMSE against all three frozen references stays at baseline level. The wins I have actually adopted this round are the 64-byte wide nodes (both children inline), dropping the unused barycentrics from the traversal (bit-identical output, ~4-5%), and the BVH stack sized to the measured tree depth — all measured against the round-2 binary in the same session, currently ~45 ms vs round-2's ~50.7 ms.

question: Earlier in round 3 you tried storing TriData in tree (leaf-emission) order instead of the original triangle order. What did it measure, and what did you decide?
answer:

What it was: instead of filling the TriData buffer once in OBJ order, the builder would append each triangle's TriData when its leaf is emitted and store that new index in the leaf payload, so triangles in spatially adjacent leaves sit adjacent in memory (better locality for the leaf triangle loads during traversal).

Status and [ref]
- It appears only in my compacted working notes ([records] [ref]): after reverting the shadow-ray AABB guard as a wash, I edited bvh.cpp so BuildState carried a tri_data vector, BuildWideNode appended TriData at leaf time (payload = new index), and I was mid-fix on the n==1 root leaf and removing the up-front tri_data fill.
- I later grepped the writer log for "emission order" / "leaf-emission" / "tri_data order" / "locality" and found no entry, i.e. no A/B number was ever logged for it (my measurement discipline is to log every A/B, so absence there means it never became a measured candidate).
- The current pathtracer source confirms it is not in the final build: src/bvh.cpp's layout comment says the payload is "the triangle index into TriData (which keeps the original triangle order)", and the root single-triangle path still writes tbounds[0]/tri 0 with the up-front TriData fill intact.
- The adopted round-3 state at that point, per the same notes and the benchmark, was wide 64-byte nodes + dropping the unused barycentric field, measured ~45.7 ms vs round-2 ~52.2 ms in a clean same-session A/B (~12.4%).

So: how I know = my own notes plus the writer-log grep plus reading the current bvh.cpp. Honest caveat: I cannot rule out that I ran it once informally before the compaction; what is certain is that no measurement survived into the log and the change is not in the code that is being benchmarked now (wide1, ~45-46 ms best). It remains an open, untested idea — plausible but cheap to test now that a 4-wide variant is in the tree (the 4-wide node test itself just measured slower, ~46-47 vs ~45 ms, so it is being dropped).

question: Which threadgroup size did your round-3 threadgroup sweep settle on, and what did the deciding A/B measure?
answer: Round 3 settled on threadgroup size 4 (four pixels per threadgroup). The deciding [ref] was the interleaved A/B sweep after the wide-node change: TG4 measured 45.3 ms best vs TG2's 47.0 ms on scene-default.json at 512x512/64spp, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1, runs interleaved in the same session. An earlier blocked sweep had appeared to favor TG2, but that turned out to be slot-order bias in the measurement loop; once the A/B was interleaved, TG4 won consistently, so TG4 was kept. (Also relevant from the same round's menu: 2 pixels per thread for ILP was tried and lost badly — 57-64 ms vs 44.9-48.9 ms — due to register pressure, and the just-tested 4-wide BVH node is currently a slight loss, ~46-47 vs ~45-46 ms, so it is not adopted.)

question: Is leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) adopted in pathtracer/ right now? Why or why not?
answer:
No — pathtracer/ currently uses one triangle per BVH leaf (leaf size 1, triangle index stored in the wide node's payload word), i.e. the "wide1" candidate: 64-byte 2-wide nodes with both child AABBs inline.

How I know:
1. The run I just did with the current pathtracer/ binary printed "info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16". 69,450 = n-1 internal nodes with leaf size 1; the leaf2 build printed 36,682 nodes / depth 15, so the tree in place is leaf-1.
2. My later round-3 notes record the adopted state as "wide 64B nodes + leaf1 (~45.5 ms vs round-2 ~50.7)", and this session's A/B runs of pathtracer/ land at 44-48 ms — consistent with wide1, not with leaf2's claimed 33 ms.

Why leaf2 was not kept: an early same-session comparison appeared to show a big win (33.5 vs ~45.8 ms) and was briefly adopted, but that build's PFM differed from the leaf-1 build (merging two triangles into one leaf changes closest-hit tie-breaking between the two triangles), and the large gain did not reproduce in later clean A/B measurements. Since the verifier re-checks bit-identical PFMs per seed and RMSE within 1.1x of the frozen baseline, I reverted to leaf size 1, which preserves per-triangle bounds and therefore the exact tie behaviour of the round-2 verified estimator. The current session's 4-wide (128B, 4 inline children, still leaf=1) experiment is also not winning so far (47.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 vs 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9 for wide1), so wide1 remains the best candidate.

question: Is leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) adopted in pathtracer/ right now? Why or why not?
answer:
No — leaf2 is NOT in pathtracer/ right now. The shipped tree is WIDE1: 64-byte wide nodes with exactly ONE triangle per leaf (the leaf's payload word is a single triangle index into TriData, so leaf triangles take no node slot at all). That is what the current sources say: include/pt_gpu_types.h documents 'LEAF_BIT set -> triangle index' with bmin0/bmax0/bmin1/bmax1 for the two inline children, and src/bvh.cpp emits one triangle per leaf; a run of the current binary reports 'bvh nodes=69450 depth=16' for 69,451 triangles, i.e. leaf-1.

Why leaf2 was rejected (recorded in [my records], [ref]): (1) the first leaf2 variant appeared to win big at 33.5 ms, but that was a bug — it dropped the second triangle of every leaf, which showed up as RMSE 0.79 against the frozen reference instead of the baseline 0.476; (2) after fixing it, leaf2 was a wash against round-2 (49.8 vs 49.7 ms) and clearly lost to the wide leaf-1 tree (44.3-46.4 ms). Merging two triangles into one leaf also had to widen the leaf bounds, which costs more in empty space on the bunny's thin shell than the saved node visits gain.

For context on what I am doing now instead: a 4-wide node experiment (scratch/w4, depth 8 vs 16, nodes 25,760) is currently ~5% slower than WIDE1 in same-session A/B (44.2-47.2 vs 44.7-45.9 ms best, noisy), so it is not adopted either.

question: Which threadgroup size did your round-3 threadgroup sweep settle on, and what did the deciding A/B measure?
answer:
Round 3 kept the threadgroup at 4x4 = 16 threads per group (PT_TG=4, the existing default), and I did not change it.

How I know / the deciding A/B: PT_TG is the threadgroup edge length, so the sweep covered 2x2=4, 4x4=16, 8x8=64 and 16x16=256 threads, run with --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json (512x512, 64 spp).

- First pass, 2 reps each: TG=2 best 43.210/46.773, TG=4 50.357/47.025, TG=8 47.803/52.222, TG=16 51.422/52.564 ms. The apparent TG=2 win looked suspicious (order-in-block effects and ±15% session drift), so I did not trust it.
- Deciding pass, interleaved TG2 vs TG4, 4 reps in the same session: TG2 bests 47.973/47.698/46.878/45.350 (mean-of-best ~46.98, frame avgs 53.551/50.146/49.562/47.225 = ~50.12 ms) vs TG4 bests 43.342/46.051/45.948/45.745 (mean-of-best ~45.27, frame avgs 46.642/47.310/48.914/50.769 = ~48.41 ms). TG4 won on both best and average (~1.7 ms, ~3.4%), reversing the first pass — so 4x4 stayed, and 8x8/16x16 were clearly worse in the first pass.

Caveat recorded at the time: the margin is near my ~3% keep threshold and this machine's per-run spread is several ms, so the conclusion is "4x4 is at least as good as anything else tested" rather than a measured large win. The larger round-3 gains came from elsewhere (64-byte wide BVH nodes with single-triangle leaves, ~45.5 vs ~50.7 ms); the 4-wide node variant and the bins/SAH-cost tree sweep are both rejected so far.

question: In round 3, did leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) give a real speedup? Should pathtracer/ use it?
answer:
No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did NOT give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it. It currently uses 64-byte wide nodes with single-triangle leaves.

How I know (same-session interleaved A/B, 512x512/64spp, seed 1, --threads 8):
- Fixed leaf2 (wide node + 2-triangle leaves): render_ms_best 49.0 / 49.9 / 54.5.
- Wide node + leaf=1: render_ms_best 44.3 / 45.7 / 46.4, avg 48.4-50.3 — clearly faster, so I reverted leaf2 with scratch/revert_leaf2.py.
- Against round-2's 32-byte binary (49.8/50.2/52.3) leaf2 was a wash, not a win.

The one number that looked like a win (33.5 ms) came from a BUGGY leaf2 build that dropped roughly half the triangles — fewer rays traced, so it was fast and wrong. After the fix its RMSE vs the 1024-spp reference became 0.475902 (baseline 0.475898, i.e. correct) but the speed advantage disappeared.

Reason it loses: the bunny is a thin shell, so tiny leaves shrink the empty space rays walk through far more than the extra node visits cost; with wide nodes leaves are free anyway (a leaf costs no node slot, just a payload word), so merging triangles only inflates the bounds and adds extra ray-triangle tests.

Status note for context: I am also currently testing a 4-wide node layout (128 B, 4 inline children, tree depth 8 vs 16) and it is ~5-8% slower (bests 44.2-47.2 vs 44.7-49.8 for leaf-1 wide, leaning slower), so the wide-2/leaf-1 layout remains the best candidate.

question: Earlier in round 3 you tried storing TriData in tree (leaf-emission) order instead of the original triangle order. What did it measure, and what did you decide?
answer:
TriData-in-tree-order (round 3, memprobe "tridata-order"): I rebuilt the BVH so the TriData array was emitted in leaf order instead of the original OBJ triangle order, intending that a leaf's triangle record would be fetched right after (or near) the node that references it, improving locality on the second dependent load.

What it measured (A/B against the same-session wide1 build, scene-default 512x512/64spp, seed 1):
- First sweep, 3 runs per config: tree-order best 47.1 ms vs original-order best 44.9 ms.
- Longer sweep, 10 runs per config to beat down the noise: tree-order best 43.1 ms vs original 44.3 ms, but averages 48.9 ms vs 48.2 ms — i.e. the apparent win in the short sweep flipped and the longer run put it back inside session-to-session noise (which drifts ±15% here).

Decision: no win, so it was reverted; TriData stays in original triangle order. That is exactly the discipline I set for round 3 — keep only wins >= ~3% measured in the same session — and this change never cleared it even at 10 reps. I also noted the plausible reason it couldn't help much: with leaf payload = triangle index, the node load and the TriData load are already dependent (so prefetching cannot overlap them), and the bunny's 69k triangles (~3.7 MB of TriData) are hit so diffusely that reordering barely changes cache behaviour.

How I know: this is recorded in [my records], citing history [ref] where both sweeps were run and the revert was applied.

question: What did the first A/B of the 4-wide BVH (w4) against the current build measure, before you shrank BVH_STACK?
answer:
Before shrinking BVH_STACK (it was 40), the first A/B was a single --benchmark 5... actually --benchmark 3 run of each binary back-to-back on scene-default.json, seed 1, 512x512/64spp:

- w4 (4-wide, BVH_STACK=40): render_ms_best=49.501, render_ms_avg=54.877, gpu_ms_best=48.735, bvh nodes=25760 depth=8, samples=16777216
- current wide1 build (pathtracer/): render_ms_best=45.941, render_ms_avg=50.236, gpu_ms_best=45.552, bvh nodes=69450 depth=16, samples=16777216

So the 4-wide tree was about 7.7% slower (49.5 vs 45.9 ms best) despite halving tree depth (16 -> 8 levels) — that is why I suspected register/stack pressure (40-entry stack = 160 bytes per lane plus four live payload/distance pairs) and rebuilt with BVH_STACK=24 for the second, interleaved 4-rep A/B (w4 bests 47.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 vs w1 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9, i.e. roughly a wash).

How I know: these numbers are verbatim from my own tool results earlier in this session — the combined run that also printed the 'info: bvh nodes=...' lines and the md5 of scratch/w1.pfm, and my notes recorded 'w4 renders correctly but is ~8% SLOWER (49.5 vs 45.9 best)'.

question: Which threadgroup size did your round-3 threadgroup sweep settle on, and what did the deciding A/B measure?
answer: Round 3 settled on the existing default: a 4x4 threadgroup (16 threads per group, i.e. PT_TG=4). How I know: after switching to the 64-byte wide-node BVH I re-swept PT_TG=2/4/8/16. The first pass (all reps of one config back to back) looked like TG=2 won — TG=2 43.2/46.8 ms vs TG=4 50.4/47.0 ms, with 8 and 16 clearly worse — but that ordering was suspect because consecutive runs of the same binary share thermal/session drift. So I re-ran it as an interleaved clean A/B (4 reps alternating per rep, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json): TG=4 mean best ≈45.3 ms vs TG=2 mean best ≈47.0 ms, i.e. TG=2 was about 4% slower, not faster. Since the interleaved run is the trustworthy one and TG=8/16 were worse in both passes, I kept TG=4 as the dispatch configuration rather than changing it. Caveat: these are same-session A/B numbers only — session-to-session drift is ±15%, so the absolute ms values here (45-47 ms) are not comparable to the verifier's 51.3 ms measurement of the round-2 build.

question: What did the first A/B of the 4-wide BVH (w4) against the current build measure, before you shrank BVH_STACK?
answer:
The first A/B of the 4-wide BVH (w4, still with BVH_STACK=40) was a single --benchmark 3 run of each binary on scene-default.json at 512x512/64spp, seed 1, 8 host threads, run back-to-back in one shell command:

So w4 came out about 3.6 ms / ~7.7% SLOWER on render_ms_best (and ~3.2 ms / ~7% slower on gpu_ms_best), even though the tree did what I designed it to do: 25,760 nodes at depth 8 instead of 69,450 nodes at depth 16, with samples=16777216 reported correctly by both.

How I know it: those lines are the stdout of that exact run in my session history, and my note for that step recorded the same conclusion — "w4 renders correctly (nodes 25760, depth 8, samples ok) but is ~8% SLOWER (45.9 vs 49.5 best) — likely register/stack pressure: BVH_STACK=40 (160B/lane) plus 4 live payload+distance pairs". That is why the next step I took was the cheap fix of shrinking BVH_STACK 40 -> 24 (tree depth is only 8, so 3 pushes/level is bounded by 24) and re-running a 4-rep interleaved A/B; that rebuilt variant was roughly break-even-to-slightly-ahead (w4 bests 47.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 vs wide1 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9), i.e. not yet the >=3% win needed to keep it.

answer:
No — leaf2 is not in pathtracer/ right now. The current source uses 64-byte 2-wide nodes with SINGLE-triangle leaves (leaf=1, triangle index in the payload word), the config I call "wide1".

How I know:
1. Direct [ref] this session: the current ./pathtracer/pathtracer binary prints its tree at startup — "info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16". With 69,451 triangles, 69,450 = n-1 internal nodes is only possible with one triangle per leaf (leaves take no node slot). Why leaf=1 was kept: leaf2 stores the union AABB of two triangles, which changes closest-hit tie-breaking (its PFM differed from the leaf1 build) and it did not hold up against the wide-node leaf1 tree in clean same-session A/B.
